subject: history
subtitle: The Mughal Empire at its height — rulers, achievements, culture, and decline.

data.targetWord: a powerful empire that ruled much of the Indian subcontinent from 1526 to the mid-1700s, founded by Babur and reaching its greatest extent under Aurangzeb

examples.en-GB: At its height, the Mughal Empire included much of modern India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and parts of Afghanistan.

data.targetWord: a ranked official in the Mughal system who served the emperor as a military commander, administrator, or noble, with their rank showing their status

examples.en-GB: A mansabdar's rank determined how many cavalry soldiers they were expected to maintain for the emperor.

data.targetWord: a land revenue assignment given to some Mughal officials, allowing them to collect income from a particular area instead of receiving a direct salary

examples.en-GB: Officials who received a jagir could collect land revenue from peasants in the assigned area to fund their service to the emperor.

data.targetWord: a province in the Mughal Empire, governed by an official appointed by the emperor

examples.en-GB: The Mughal Empire was divided into subahs, each managed by a governor responsible to the emperor.

data.targetWord: a local landholder or revenue collector in the Mughal Empire who could support or resist central Mughal authority

examples.en-GB: Zamindars were crucial intermediaries between the Mughal state and local peasant communities.

data.targetWord: a tax on non-Muslim subjects in some Islamic states; in Mughal India it was abolished by Akbar and later reintroduced by Aurangzeb in 1679

examples.en-GB: Akbar abolished the jizya to help unite his diverse empire, while Aurangzeb reintroduced it as part of his stricter religious policies.

data.targetWord: the 'House of Worship' created by Akbar at Fatehpur Sikri where scholars and religious figures from different faiths could debate ideas

examples.en-GB: The Ibadat Khana brought together Muslim, Hindu, Jain, and Christian scholars to debate religion in Akbar's court.

data.targetWord: a white marble mausoleum built by Emperor Shah Jahan at Agra between 1632 and 1653, as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, now a symbol of Mughal architecture

examples.en-GB: The Taj Mahal is one of the finest examples of Mughal architecture, combining Persian, Central Asian, and Indian styles.

data.targetWord: a highly detailed small-scale painting produced at the Mughal court, depicting rulers, court scenes, nature, and historical events

examples.en-GB: Mughal miniature paintings are valuable historical evidence showing court life, clothing, ceremonies, and the way rulers wanted to be seen.

data.targetWord: a blue dye produced from plants in north India and traded across Asia, Africa, and Europe; one of the most valuable Mughal export goods

examples.en-GB: Indigo produced in north India was in great demand from cloth-makers in Europe, making it a hugely profitable trade good.

data.targetWord: the English trading company founded in 1600 that originally sought permission to trade in India, later growing into a powerful political and military force

examples.en-GB: When the East India Company arrived in India in the early 1600s, it was not powerful enough to conquer anything and had to ask local rulers for trading permission.

data.targetWord: the founder of the Mughal Empire, who won the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 against Ibrahim Lodi using gunpowder weapons and cavalry tactics

examples.en-GB: Babur came from Central Asia and claimed descent from Timur and Genghis Khan, giving his new dynasty great prestige.

data.targetWord: Mughal emperor from 1556 to 1605, known for expanding the empire, reforming administration, forming alliances with Hindu Rajput rulers, and encouraging religious debate

examples.en-GB: Akbar's policies of including non-Muslims in government and abolishing the jizya helped him rule a diverse empire more successfully.

data.targetWord: Mughal emperor from 1628 to 1658, famous for commissioning great architectural works including the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort in Delhi

examples.en-GB: Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal as a magnificent tomb for his beloved wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631.

data.targetWord: Mughal emperor from 1658 to 1707, who expanded the empire to its greatest territorial extent but faced serious challenges including long wars and religious tensions

examples.en-GB: Aurangzeb's long campaigns in the Deccan expanded Mughal territory but exhausted the empire's resources and finances.

data.targetWord: the influential wife of Emperor Jahangir who played an important role in court politics, patronage, and imperial decision-making

examples.en-GB: Nur Jahan's political influence shows that women in Mughal royal households could shape important decisions, even when formal power was held by men.

data.targetWord: a key official under Akbar associated with important land revenue reforms that attempted to measure land, estimate crop yields, and set more systematic taxation

examples.en-GB: Todar Mal's revenue reforms under Akbar helped make Mughal taxation more organised, though they varied greatly across regions.

data.targetWord: a religion that began in Punjab in the late 1400s with Guru Nanak and developed its own distinct identity during the Mughal period

examples.en-GB: Sikh communities became increasingly important in Punjab during the Mughal period, sometimes coming into conflict with Mughal authority.

data.targetWord: the decisive battle of 1526 in which Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, using cavalry and gunpowder weapons, establishing Mughal rule in north India

examples.en-GB: Babur's victory at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 marked the beginning of Mughal rule in India.

data.targetWord: the 1757 battle in which the East India Company defeated the Nawab of Bengal, marking the beginning of British political dominance in India

examples.en-GB: The Battle of Plassey in 1757 came long after the strongest period of Mughal power, showing how the empire had weakened after 1707.

data.targetWord: Akbar's planned city, built near Agra, which served as the Mughal capital for a time and was associated with religious debate and imperial display

examples.en-GB: Fatehpur Sikri, with its Ibadat Khana for religious debate, shows Akbar's interest in bringing different faiths together at his court.

data.targetWord: cloth or fabric; Mughal India was a major producer of cotton and silk textiles that were traded across Asia, Africa, and Europe

examples.en-GB: Indian cotton textiles were so popular across the world that European trading companies travelled thousands of miles to buy them.

data.targetWord: the long-term impact or lasting influence of a person, event, period, or civilisation on later generations

examples.en-GB: The legacy of Mughal architecture can still be seen today in the Taj Mahal and Red Fort, which attract millions of visitors each year.

data.targetWord: Hindu warrior clans from Rajasthan who became important allies of the Mughal Empire, especially under Akbar's policy of marriage alliances

examples.en-GB: Akbar's alliances with Rajput rulers through marriage helped stabilise Mughal rule by bringing powerful Hindu elites into the imperial system.

data.targetWord: Aurangzeb's long military campaigns to expand and control the Deccan plateau in central and southern India, which proved enormously costly

examples.en-GB: The Deccan campaigns stretched the Mughal army and treasury for decades, contributing to the empire's weakening after Aurangzeb's death in 1707.

data.title: Put the Mughal emperors in order from first to last
items: Humayun — lost and regained power, died 1556
Akbar — expanded and stabilised the empire (1556-1605)
Jahangir — associated with court culture and painting (1605-1627)
Shah Jahan — built the Taj Mahal (1628-1658)
Aurangzeb — expanded to greatest extent, died 1707

data.title: Order the cause-and-consequence chain for Mughal stability under Akbar
items: Mughal Empire rules a religiously diverse population
Akbar recognises that force alone cannot govern such diversity
Akbar forms marriage alliances with Rajput rulers
Akbar abolishes the jizya and encourages religious debate
Non-Muslim elites are included in government and military
The empire gains broader support and becomes more stable

data.title: Order the sequence of Mughal decline
items: Aurangzeb launches costly campaigns to conquer the Deccan
Long wars stretch the army and exhaust the treasury
Aurangzeb dies in 1707 leaving a weakened empire
Regional powers grow stronger and challenge Mughal authority
East India Company takes advantage of political divisions
Battle of Plassey in 1757 — Company gains power in Bengal
